extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers/experimental scientists (readers of the Royal Society; 17th-century experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and practical/principled statements from 17th-century Philosophical Transactions articles on acoustics (otacoustics), salt crystallization, sea-plant distillation, hygroscopicity of oil of vitriol, and pyritic origins of thunder/earthquakes; intended to guide observation, experiment design, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of medium surface on sound propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: The smooth surface of the water conveys a sound more entire, and to a greater distance than the plane surface of a piece of ground, a wall, or any other solid body whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smooth, continuous media (water) transmit sound more completely and farther than uneven or plane solid surfaces; this should be taken into account when predicting or measuring audibility over distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ear placement near surfaces improves hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The organ, which is the ear, is helped much by placing it near a wall, especially at one end of an arch, when the sound is produced at the other, or near the surface of water, or of the earth, along which the sounds are most easily and naturally conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximity to appropriate reflecting or conducting surfaces (walls, arches, water, ground) can increase effective hearing; experimental setups or demonstrations should consider ear placement to observe maximal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refracted hearing due to changes in medium density
rubrics_metrics.description: As any object seen through a thickened air by refraction appears larger, so likewise a sound, heard through the same thickened part of the atmosphere, will be considerably varied from what it would seem to be if heard through a thinner medium — called a refracted sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density, figure, and magnitude of the medium, and incidence of rays (analogous for sound), alter perception; when studying long-range or distorted hearing, account for refractive variations in atmospheric layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental assistance for sending and receiving sound (otacoustics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments may be contrived for assisting both the sonorous body, to send forth its sound more strongly, and the acoustic faculty to receive and discern it more easily and clearly — analogues to spectacles, telescopes, microscopes, polyscopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design goals: (a) project the voice or source to greater distance and loudness (like a burning-glass for light); (b) magnify faint sounds (microphones/micracoustics) so minute noises become audible; (c) multiply or distribute sound (polyphones) to simulate many instruments or voices. Use optical instrument analogies as conceptual templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for reflected audition (echoes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sound falling directly or obliquely on any dense body of a smooth surface is beat back again and reflected; but if the sound be propagated parallel to the surface of the dense body there will be no reflection of sound, no echo. If the surface be uneven, reverberation will break and extinguish the sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce clear echoes, ensure smooth reflecting surfaces and non-parallel incidence; uneven surfaces and reverberatory air motion destroy precise echoes. Receiver position matters — reflected sound may pass over or under the originator and be heard elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between obstacle shape and echoed sound
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) A plane obstacle reflects the sound back in its due tone and loudness (allowing for distance attenuation). 2) A convex obstacle repels the sound smaller but somewhat quicker. 3) A concave obstacle echoes back the sound louder, slower, and also inverted; but never according to the order of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or interpreting echoes, consider obstacle geometry: plane → faithful but attenuated reflection; convex → diminished/quicker return; concave → amplified/slowed/inverted returns (note inversion does not preserve word order). Use these distinctions when constructing rooms or echo experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance and placement control quantity of echo repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A reflecting body being removed farther off reflects more of the sound than when nearer; this is the reason why some echoes repeat but one syllable, some one word, and some many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amount of reproduced material (syllable/word/phrase) depends on apparent magnitude and distance of reflecting surface — arrange distances to control echo content and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple and successive echoes by arranging echoing bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Echoing bodies may be so contrived and placed, that reflecting the sound from one to the other, either directly and mutually, or obliquely and by succession, out of one sound shall many echoes be produced; a multiple echo may be made by placing echoing bodies at unequal distances that reflect all one way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create manifold successive sounds (e.g., one clap like many), place multiple reflecting surfaces at differing distances and orientations so reflections do not cancel and return in succession; this can simulate ensembles or create acoustical effects in performance spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering problems for otacoustics (explicit instrument goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three proposed problems: (1) make the least sound, by the help of instruments, as loud as the greatest; (2) propagate any the least sound to the greatest distance; (3) convey a sound from one extreme to the other so as not to be heard in the middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete design targets: (1) extreme amplification of faint sources; (2) extreme distance propagation; (3) highly directional transmission (privacy/targeted communication). Use them as success criteria for proposed acoustic inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea-salt vs inland common salt crystal morphology as diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: The angles of the crystals of common salt boiled out of the midland brine-pits are entire; but some of the angles of the crystals of true sea salt are always cut off into triangular planes, at least on one of the sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification method: evaporate sea-water leisurely (shade, after partially boiling) and inspect crystal shapes. Reproducible formation of triangular-capped crystals indicates marine origin; repeat experiment to confirm universality across samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation of sweet water by breath of sea plants (experimental method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filling a long glass body with sea-water and putting in fresh sea-weed, covering with a receiver without lute or closing joints, daily distilled a fresh, very sweet, and potable water from the plants' breath (humidity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method for obtaining potable water from sea-water without fire-distillation: use living sea-plants in a closed but not airtight glass apparatus to collect plant-exhaled distillate; observe taste (no empyreuma) and consider use for navigators. Repeatability noted by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hygroscopic uptake of oil of vitriol measured by serial weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure of oil of vitriol (sulphuric acid) unstopped in an open glass and placed on a scale yielded measurable increase in weight over successive natural days; diary of hourly/periodic gains recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: place known quantity in open glass on sensitive scales, record mass at intervals, keep environmental notes (weather, wind, time) to correlate; this yields a hygroscopicity diary and supports quantitative conclusions about moisture uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moisture is chief cause of weight increase in oil of vitriol
rubrics_metrics.description: From the diary and observations, it is obvious that the more the liquor was saturated the less was its daily increase; the increase was more in moist, rainy, misty, and snowy season, but less in frosty, clear, and dry one. Hence moisture is the chief and only cause of the increase of weight in oil of vitriol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting hygroscopic weight change, prioritize ambient humidity as primary driver; control for season, local dryness/moisture, and expect larger uptake in damp conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors influencing vitriol weight gain (strength, surface area, season, position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of total increase varies with the strength (dilution) of the oil of vitriol; more diluted liquids are less attractive. Also season, position of place (cellar vs room), and proportion of surface to bulk strongly influence rate and total uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments controlling for concentration and surface-area-to-volume ratio; expect smaller surface → slower uptake and much longer times to saturation. Consider placement (sunless cellar increases uptake) when using vitriol as a hygroscope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-area-to-bulk proportion dictates speed of hygroscopic increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater or less surface is the quicker or slower the increase: 3 drams in open flat glass 1 inch broad gained far less in 6 hours than same quantity spread on a broader surface; time of increasing bears near exact proportion to the surface of the liquor exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accelerate hygroscopic adsorption for measurement or for making a sensitive hygroscope, maximize exposed surface area; small-area samples take many times longer to saturate and show smaller short-term gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of oil of vitriol as a hygroscope (instrument design suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A balance with oil of vitriol in a concave glass can serve as a hygroscope; suggested contrivances include: (a) balance pin in middle with a long tapering tongue pointing to divisions on an arched plate; (b) scale hung near the pin with the other end long to mark large arch on a board. Inscribe temperature divisions on the arches; other liquids (oil of sulphur, oil of tartar, liquor of fixed nitre) may also succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical construction details: use small concave glass pans, long indicator tongues/arcs to magnify minute weight changes, calibrate divisions against known temperatures/humidity; alternative designs (viol-string index) proposed for increased sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative hygroscope design using viol-string length change
rubrics_metrics.description: A hygroscope might be made of a viol-string running over pulleys, suspending a bullet connected to the shorter end of an index, the other extremity long to describe a long arch by the rising and falling of the bullet, the index fastened to the centre of the last pulley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical hygroscope exploiting hygroscopic length change: use string tension change to move an index over an arc — can be highly sensitive if arranged with suitable levers/pulleys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrites (sulphur) as proposed material cause of thunder, lightning, and earthquakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The breath of the pyrites, which is sulphur, naturally takes fire of itself; the material cause of thunder and lightning and of earthquakes is the inflammable breath of the pyrites — difference being one fired in the air, the other under ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis for natural phenomena: seek sulphurous smell, inflammable vapours, and pyritic deposits as indicators; consider subterranean cavities filled with inflammable vapours as loci for earthquakes. Use these signatures as criteria when evaluating claims about causes of thunder/earthquakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence supporting pyritic origin (smell, noise, mine damps, cavities, pyrites distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporting observations include: burned objects and brimstone smell from lightning; sulphurous stink of waters before earthquakes; noises like a train fired; damp 'damps' in mines; presence and varying richness of pyrites in minerals and in volcanic regions versus regions with fewer earthquakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the pyrite hypothesis, collect multimodal evidence: olfactory (sulphurous smell), acoustic (train-like noises), geological (natural cavities, pyrites frequency), and mining observations (damps). Compare distribution of pyrites with regional earthquake incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances used as extraordinary supporting evidence (rain of iron, magnetic lightning effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorded instances include iron or iron-stone falling from the air and lightning producing magnetic effects (compass needles changing polarity); a petrified piece of ash found magnetic is cited as evidence that vapour may carry magnetic/pyritic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such extraordinary reports as potential empirical supports to be investigated: verify physical specimens (e.g., 'aes nubigenum'), test magnetism of lightning-affected objects, and attempt reproducible documentation before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed effect of lightning on compasses (field report)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account: ship encountering a thunder storm — lightning burned sails/masts and something bituminous fell on stern; afterwards compasses showed altered needles (north point turned south or west); one affected compass lost its virtue after glass broke and air accessed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logged nautical incidents as field data: when lightning strikes, record instrument changes (compass readings, physical damage, residues), preserve affected needles for analysis; consider lightning's capacity to magnetize or demagnetize compass needles as evidence relating to the magnetic nature of lightning or deposited material.
